newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean president's apology sparks more anger.
newsitem.headline: South Korean president's apology sparks more anger.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam sought to rescue his administration by apologising on Friday over election spending abuses, but his comments only fuelled the anger of his opponents.
Kim's statement, broadcast live on national television, offered no specifics and fell far short of the act of personal contrition demanded by the opposition.

Opposition groups allege that Kim's 1992 presidential campaign was partly bankrolled by the scandal-ridden Hanbo Group and far exceeded legal spending limits. They demanded to know exactly how much he spent, and who gave him the money.
Kim noted that the issue of his 1992 spending had been "raised as a problem in political circles".
"For this, first of all, I and our entire political circle must bow our heads to the public and repent of past wrongdoings," he said.
"I'm sure you understand that it is impossible to reveal the entire size of funds and spending from five years ago during a hectic election campaign," a solemn-faced Kim said.

Kim, whose credibility has been shattered by the campaign financing furore and a related bribery scandal involving senior aides and his own son, called on all political parties to draft new legislation to combat funding irregularities.
An earlier refusal to detail his spending sparked public outrage and veiled calls for his resignation.
"President Kim's speech ended by avoiding and shifting all responsibility," said a spokeswoman for the largest opposition party, the National Congress for New Politics.
"We will use all means to fight to reveal the truth," said Park Sun-suck.

"We will try to call President Kim Young-sam to a National Assembly hearing as a witness," she said, adding that her party would join hands with the smaller United Liberal Democrats in their battle against the head of state.
At one point, Kim even appeared combative, chastising opposition parties for dwelling on the issue. Opposition leaders are widely believed to have abused the system, too.

"If you really worry about the difficulties this country faces, and if you really regret the faulty political climate, I hope you will stop the national drift with wasteful discussions of the election funds," Kim said.
He was referring to the faltering economy, which has added to the sense of national crisis.
The president's immediate woes stem from the collapse in January of Hanbo Steel Co, which uncovered a web of corruption linking the company to his top aides and bankers.
Prosecutors allege that politicians took kickbacks from Hanbo in return for arranging loans worth five trillion won ($5.6 billion) to the country's second largest steelmaker.

Kim apologised for a second time over the so-called "Hanbogate" scandal, which also led to the arrest of his own son, Kim Hyun-chul. He first expressed his remorse in a televised speech to the nation in February.
"The results of the 'Hanbo incident' showed all of us the depth of the roots of corruption and the links between business and politics," Kim said.
Kim called on all parties to revise laws relating to campaign spending.
If that failed through political self-interest, he said: "I will have no choice but to make a grave resolution." He did not elaborate.
